text.p: Anaconda Nickel Ltd chief executive Andrew Forrest, speaking in an aboriginal tribal language at a seminar, called on the mining industry on Thursday to reconcile its differences over aboriginal land rights.

Speaking in the Wong Utha Wongi language on behalf of what he called the aboriginal voice of the north-eastern gold fields of Western Australia, Forrest said aboriginals needed opportunities to reach total reconciliation.

"We need companies and governments to provide careers, contracts and the education and training to go with it, so that only then can we become equal, only then can we achieve equality and reconciliation in a true sense," Forrest told a seminar.
Forrest later provided a translated version of his speech, delivered at the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE) Outlook conference.
Forrest, who is developing the Murrin Murrin nickel/cobalt project in Western Australia, said the project will employ about 20 percent aboriginals out of a total workforce of about 350.

Forrest said he had been exposed to the aboriginal culture as a child when he lived on a remote sheep station in the Western Australian desert. "For the first 10 years of my life, 90 percent of my mates were aboriginal," he said.

Forrest said Anaconda has reached its own agreements with aboriginal land claimants over tracts of the Murrin Murrin project. "You have given lawyers and a few selfish people amongst the rights to cripple projects through delays, the rights to great big long negotiating periods, the rights to the High Court and its many appeal processes," he said in the Wong Utha Wongi language. -- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 373-1800
